result:
Not quite. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own, so your assistant won't automatically remember what students told it last week.

The model only sees the text in front of it on each call, which is its context. When a conversation ends, nothing stays inside the model. Chatbots seem to remember because the app resends the earlier messages with every new one. A new session starts blank unless your code does something about it.

Here is how that plays out for the makerspace:

- Last week, Sam tells the assistant "I finished the laser cutter training."
- This week, Sam asks to book the laser cutter. The model has no idea who Sam is or what Sam said.
- For it to know, your code has to save that fact somewhere, such as a database row or a JSON file. Next session, it has to load the fact and put it into the context, or give the model a tool that looks it up.

So memory is a design decision in your system, not a built-in property of the model. That also affects your budget, because everything you put back into the context costs tokens on every call.

This is the topic your notes list as next, and it ties directly to your mission goal of deciding what the assistant keeps in its context and what it saves between sessions. I can write a 15-minute lesson on it if you'd like.

Quick check: if the assistant is going to know Sam's training status next week, which part of your system has to store it, the model or your code?
